name: Fatima Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the livestock lead at Greenhollow, a co-operative farm owned by about forty members, me included with one small share. We've 70 dairy cows, a bit of wheat and oats, and a farm shop that sells our milk and yoghurt. I'm in the parlour by half five, then calves, then feed planning, then whatever meeting the co-op has dreamed up that week. I love the calves. I could do without the meetings, though I'd defend them to anyone.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being the person in between. The board wants costs down, the younger members want everything organic, and the cows just want to be milked on time. My partner Sam works at the council roads depot, and our two, Yusuf and Mira, are eleven and eight. I do use one of those AI chat tools now and then, mostly to tidy up grant forms, because I hate writing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Some of the board would be disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop talking about it and get on with milking. Half our meetings last year were about whether to buy a robot milker. I'd post something cheerful in the co-op group chat, probably a picture of a cow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. My job's safe, our members keep their say, and I keep using the chat tool for grant forms, which saves me maybe two evenings a quarter. The things that actually worry me, milk prices and feed costs, are the same as ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd probably push the co-op to spend the robot milker money on a new calf shed instead, about 40,000 we'd been setting aside. At home we'd keep putting 200 a month into savings like we already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, maybe, because I'd got used to the idea of something big coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those two evenings the AI saves you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the two evenings the AI saves me, I'd sit at my daughter Mira's swimming lessons without a laptop on my knee. That sounds small, but it's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the co-op who'd be disappointed it fizzled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, our youngest member, would be gutted. He's been reading about robot weeders for two years and he'd have to find a new hobby. I'd buy him a pint and tell him the calf shed is exciting too.

S0.say: Good, now we can stop talking about it and get on with milking. Half our meetings last year were about whether to buy a robot milker.
S0.think: It suits me fine: my job's safe and our members keep their say. The things that really worry me, milk prices and feed costs, stay the same.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is and pushes the co-op to spend the robot milker fund, about 40,000, on a new calf shed. Keeps saving 200 a month at home.
S0.feel: Calm, and slightly flat after expecting something big.
S0.quote: With the two evenings the AI saves me, I'd sit at my daughter Mira's swimming lessons without a laptop on my knee.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima sees the co-op's structure as a buffer, and expects her real worries to stay economic. She uses AI modestly and values the time it saves for family. She already thinks in terms of what the co-op should vote for.

steps.text: Push the co-op to spend the 40,000 robot milker fund on a new calf shed
Keep milking the 70 cows and using the chat tool for grant forms
Keep putting 200 a month into the family savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to make sure the co-op decides how the robots come in, not the machinery dealer. I'd say it to the members and probably on the farmers' forum. Change is fine if the people doing the work have a vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes more than it disappears. A robot milker would take my mornings, but someone still has to know when a cow's off her feed. I'd go from milking to managing data and health, and I'm not sure I'd like that as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until two or three farms near us have had robot milkers running for a year, then back the co-op buying one. I'd go on the dealer's two-day training and learn the herd software properly. And I'd ask the union to negotiate what happens to the two part-time milkers we employ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can manage. It's change, not loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to those two part-time milkers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me awake in this one. Grace has worked with us for nine years and she's 58, so she's not going to retrain into software. I'd fight for the co-op to keep her on for calf work, even if it costs us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure you'd like the job as much. What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warmth, honestly. Nothing beats standing between two cows on a January morning with your hands on a warm flank. You don't get that from a screen showing yield graphs.

S1.say: The co-op should decide how robots come in, not the machinery dealer. Change is fine if the people doing the work have a vote on it.
S1.think: My job changes more than it disappears: a robot milker takes my mornings, but someone still has to know when a cow is off her feed. I'm not sure I'd enjoy the data side as much.
S1.do: Waits until nearby farms have run robot milkers for a year, then backs the co-op buying one and does the dealer's two-day training. Asks the union to negotiate the future of the two part-time milkers.
S1.feel: Uneasy but manageable, more change than loss.
S1.quote: Nothing beats standing between two cows on a January morning with your hands on a warm flank. You don't get that from a screen showing yield graphs.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima is a classic 'once it's proven' adopter and puts her trust in co-op votes and union deals. Her strongest worry was for Grace, a 58-year-old colleague, not herself. She expects to miss the physical warmth of the work.

steps.text: Wait until two or three nearby farms have run robot milkers for a year
Take the dealer's two-day training and learn the herd software properly
Ask the union to negotiate the future of the co-op's two part-time milkers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for the hands. Our board takes two years to choose a paint colour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the members we have three years between the AI and the robots, and that's exactly the time a co-op needs if we start now. I'd put a motion to the spring meeting to set up a planning group for it. Online I'd say the same thing, that farms owned by the people who work them have to plan together or the big dairies will plan for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my mornings in the parlour are safe until about 2031, but my feed planning and the grant forms are gone in 2028. That's maybe a third of my week, and it's the part that gets me the title of livestock lead. Then in 2031 the big robot dairies start selling milk cheaper than we can, and I don't know if forty members can agree fast enough to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd start using the AI properly for feed plans, not just grant forms, because by then it would be proven and I'd be daft not to. I'd get the planning group going and push the co-op to start a robot fund now, even if it means the calf shed waits again. At home we'd put the 200 a month toward the mortgage instead of savings, to get the balance down before Sam's job at the roads depot goes the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. If I've got a list and a meeting date, I can carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Sam's job. What happens at the roads depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam drives a gritter and patches potholes, so that's hands-on too, and the council would probably wait for the robots. But the depot's rotas and orders would go to the AI in 2028, and his supervisor already talks about cutting staff. So we'd have two jobs on the same three-year clock, which is the bit I'd stare at the ceiling about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Grace, the part-time milker you worried about before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would be 63 by 2031, close enough to her pension that a co-op could carry her for two years if we wanted to. I'd make sure the planning group put Grace's job in writing as the first thing we protect. If a co-op can't look after a woman who's milked its cows for nine years, what's the point of a co-op?

S2.say: We have three years between the AI and the robots, and that's exactly the time a co-op needs if we start now. Farms owned by the people who work them have to plan together, or the big dairies will plan for us.
S2.think: My parlour mornings are safe until about 2031, but the feed planning and grant forms go in 2028, and that's the part that makes me livestock lead. Then the big robot dairies start undercutting us, and I don't know if forty members can agree fast enough.
S2.do: Starts using AI for feed plans as soon as it's proven, and sets up a co-op planning group with a robot fund, even if the calf shed waits again. Moves the family's 200 a month from savings to paying down the mortgage before Sam's depot job is hit too.
S2.feel: Anxious, but the busy kind. With a list and a meeting date she can carry it.
S2.quote: If a co-op can't look after a woman who's milked its cows for nine years, what's the point of a co-op?
S2.fieldNote: Fatima split her job in two straight away: the planning part that goes in 2028 and the parlour work that lasts to 2031. Her real worry is her household having two jobs on the same three-year clock, since Sam's depot work follows the same pattern. Her instinct under pressure is to organise, and she puts the oldest worker first.

steps.text: Use the AI for Greenhollow's feed plans, not just grant forms
Set up a co-op planning group and a robot fund at the spring meeting
Put the 200 a month toward the mortgage before Sam's depot job changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five and eight years. That's a co-op-sized timeline, just about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where co-ops can actually win, because we'd have time to buy machines together and share them. I'd say it at the members' meeting and on the farmers' forum. I'd also say the government should help small farms buy in groups, not just hand grants to the big estates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out of this one all right if I move in the first two years. I'd be 51 when the robots arrive, and a co-op will still need someone who knows the cows to run the machines and spot a sick heifer. The danger is me waiting too long because waiting is what I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the herd health course at the agricultural college in the second year, evenings, once a couple of people I know have done it. I'd push the co-op to share a robot milker with the Fernley co-op down the valley rather than each buying one. We'd keep saving 200 a month and leave the kitchen for another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared. It's a long enough run-up that I can see myself landing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said waiting is what you always do. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work somewhere I trust. When Fernley got their first robot weeder, I went and stood in their field for an afternoon before I'd say a word at our meeting. If the AI was running their herd plans by 2032 and the cows looked fine, I'd be first in the queue after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf and Mira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf would be sixteen when the robots came, so he'd be choosing his subjects. I'd tell my son to learn how the machines work and how animals work, both, because nobody seems to know both. Mira would still think it's all about the calves, and I'd let her.

S3.say: This is the version where co-ops can actually win, because we'd have time to buy machines together and share them. The government should help small farms buy in groups, not just hand grants to the big estates.
S3.think: I think I'd come out all right if I move in the first two years, because a co-op will still need someone who knows the cows to run the machines. The danger is me waiting too long, because waiting is what I always do.
S3.do: Signs up for an evening herd health course at the agricultural college in year two, once people she knows have done it. Pushes Greenhollow to share a robot milker with the Fernley co-op, keeps saving 200 a month and puts off the new kitchen.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more curious than scared. The run-up is long enough that she can see herself landing it.
S3.quote: I'd tell my son to learn how the machines work and how animals work, both, because nobody seems to know both.
S3.fieldNote: Fatima knows her own habit of waiting for proof and names it as the main risk here. She has a clear test: watch the Fernley co-op try it first. The eight years to robots let her picture a future role running machines rather than being replaced by them.

steps.text: Take the evening herd health course at the agricultural college in year two
Push Greenhollow to share a robot milker with the Fernley co-op
Keep saving 200 a month and put off the new kitchen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until a robot can do my job. I'd be 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got no excuse not to get this right, and I'd want the co-op federation to have a plan on paper within two years. In public I'd keep it upbeat. Ten years is enough time to bring the machines in on our terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the risk with ten years is that nobody does anything for eight of them. Our board has put off a new calf shed for six years running, so I know how a long deadline goes. For me personally, 56 with a herd health skill and a share in the co-op doesn't sound too bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the first few years run as normal and use the AI tools when the co-op does. I'd put 40 a month each into education funds for Yusuf and Mira. And I'd join the co-op federation's policy group, because that's where the shared-machine rules would get written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm on the surface, a bit uneasy underneath. Mostly I worry about everyone else putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Grace would be retired by 2039. Who would you worry about instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, funnily enough, the young one who loves robot weeders. He'd be in his thirties and the machines he dreamed about would be the ones doing his job. He thinks he'll be the one running them, but there won't be many of those jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the first years run as normal. Isn't that what you worry the board will do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. I'd be doing exactly what I complain about. I suppose the difference is I'd be saving and planning on paper, and the board would be doing nothing at all. That's a thin difference, I know.

S4.say: We've got no excuse not to get this right, and ten years is enough time to bring the machines in on our terms. The co-op federation should have a plan on paper within two years.
S4.think: The risk with ten years is that nobody does anything for eight of them, like our board putting off the calf shed for six years. For me personally, being 56 with a herd health skill and a co-op share doesn't sound too bad.
S4.do: Lets the first few years run as normal and adopts AI tools when the co-op does. Puts 40 a month each into education funds for Yusuf and Mira and joins the co-op federation's policy group to help write shared-machine rules.
S4.feel: Calm on the surface and a little uneasy underneath, mostly about other people putting it off.
S4.quote: Our board has put off a new calf shed for six years running, so I know how a long deadline goes.
S4.fieldNote: Fatima expects herself to be fine but distrusts what a long deadline does to an organisation. When I pointed out she'd also wait, she agreed at once. Her worry shifted from older Grace to young Jonah, whose hopes are tied to the very machines that would replace him.

steps.text: Run the dairy as normal and adopt AI tools when the co-op does
Put 40 a month each into education funds for Yusuf and Mira
Join the co-op federation's policy group on shared-machine rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam's job and mine would both be on the same three-year clock, and the co-op couldn't move fast enough before the robot dairies undercut us. What would help is public money for co-ops to buy robots together and keep their people, and a basic income while families like ours adjust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked what happens to the animals. Everyone talks about jobs. But a cow that's been handled by the same person for years notices when that person's gone.

headlineQuote: A cow that's been handled by the same person for years notices when that person's gone.
portrait: Fatima Walsh, 43, is livestock lead at Greenhollow, a members' co-operative dairy, and holds one small share. She uses an AI chat tool now and then for grant forms and trusts co-op votes and union deals to steer change. She's calm if AI stalls and uneasy with steady change, mostly worrying for an older colleague. Fast AGI makes her anxious because it takes her planning work in 2028 and puts both her parlour job and her partner's depot job on a three-year clock, so she would organise a co-op robot fund at once. With five or ten years she would retrain in herd health and share machines with a neighbouring co-op, though she admits her habit of waiting is her biggest risk.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her job and her partner's would both be on the same three-year clock and the co-op couldn't move fast enough before robot dairies undercut it.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for co-ops to buy robots together and keep their workers, plus a basic income while families adjust.
